nature-nbs-334.title: Phytoremediation: plants that clean contaminated ground
nature-nbs-334.text:
Tobacco plants given bacterial nitroreductase genes removed TNT faster. That is phytoremediation: the use of living plants to clean up soil, air and water contaminated with pollutants. Its main mechanisms are phytoextraction, phytostabilization, phytovolatilization and phytofiltration.

It is proposed as a sustainable alternative to conventional remediation, though it has never been used at large scales. Microbial bioremediation has so far been more successful. Breeding and genetic engineering can strengthen or add the abilities involved. Plant growth-promoting bacteria in the rhizosphere, the soil zone around roots, improve the results by raising biomass and by making heavy metals more mobile.

nature-nbs-341.title: Monitoring and evaluation: checking that a project works
nature-nbs-341.text:
Impact assessment after a project ends is rare, because of its cost and the difficulty of showing the project caused the results. Monitoring and evaluation are management processes that organizations use to improve their outputs, outcomes and impact. Monitoring is continuous assessment giving early information on progress or delay, so deficiencies can be corrected quickly.

Evaluation is a systematic, objective examination of relevance, effectiveness, efficiency, impact and sustainability against objectives, and it also checks that funds are well managed. Indicators must be chosen before implementation; an outcome indicator has a baseline and a target. The credibility of reports depends heavily on the independence of the evaluators.

nature-nbs-335.title: Phytoextraction: harvesting pollutants in plant shoots
nature-nbs-335.text: Phytoextraction is a {{ref:nature-nbs-334}} process in which plants take up contaminants from soil or water and concentrate them in above-ground biomass. Non-hyperaccumulators such as poplar and willow take up little pollutant but grow fast enough that they could remove a considerable amount. Heavy metals are often not mobile enough for uptake, which prompted assisted phytoextraction, adding a chelator to raise metal solubility. Metallophytes underpin phytomining, a proposed way to collect valuable metals without excavating.

nature-nbs-340.title: Phytoscreening: trees as pollution sensors
nature-nbs-340.text: A tree trunk can reveal what lies beneath it. Phytoscreening uses plants as biosensors of subsurface contamination to delineate contaminant plumes. Chlorinated solvents such as trichloroethylene have been seen in tree trunks at concentrations related to groundwater concentrations, and trunk sections are taken with an increment borer. It could optimize site investigations and lower cleanup costs, but it has achieved no practical application so far.

nature-nbs-336.title: Phytostabilization: holding pollutants in place
nature-nbs-336.text: Phytostabilization lowers the mobility of pollutants by holding them in the soil near the roots rather than in plant tissue. It aims at long-term containment and reduces erosion, runoff, leaching and the bioavailability of the contaminant. A vegetative cap has been used to stabilize and contain mine tailings. It is a form of {{ref:nature-nbs-334}} that contains a problem rather than removing it.

nature-nbs-337.title: Phytostimulation: roots that feed pollutant-eating microbes
nature-nbs-337.text: Phytostimulation enhances soil microbial activity near roots to degrade organic contaminants; it is also called rhizodegradation. It occurs in the rhizosphere, where plants release carbohydrates and acids that stimulate microorganisms to biodegrade organic contaminants. It has been tested with petroleum, PCBs and PAHs. Here the plant does not take the pollutant in; it feeds the microbes that do the breaking down.

nature-nbs-338.title: Phytovolatilization: sending pollutants into the air
nature-nbs-338.text: In phytovolatilization, plants remove substances from soil or water and release them into the air as more volatile or less polluting forms. Selenium and mercury can be removed from soil this way, selenium as dimethyl selenide and mercury as the element.

nature-nbs-339.title: Rhizofiltration: cleaning water through a web of roots
nature-nbs-339.text: Rhizofiltration filters water through a mass of roots to remove toxic substances or excess nutrients. Pollutants stay absorbed in or adsorbed to the roots. It is often used on contaminated groundwater, in place or off-site.

nature-nbs-329.title: Floods: when water covers dry land
nature-nbs-329.text:
Floods caused agricultural losses above USD 1.5 trillion between 1991 and 2023, the most destructive hazard type for global agriculture. A flood is an overflow of water that submerges land that is usually dry. It can follow prolonged heavy rain, fast snowmelt, high tides, tsunamis, or the failure of dams, levees and retention ponds. Impervious surfaces and wildfires make floods worse. A flash flood rises rapidly with little warning, usually from intense rain over a small area or on already saturated ground.

People raise the odds. Human changes such as deforestation, wetland removal, rerouted waterways and levees often raise the intensity and frequency of flooding. Coincident events, such as warm rain melting snowpack or ice and debris blocking channels, can make extreme floods more frequent than simple rainfall-runoff statistics predict. Flood statistics estimate the 100-year flood from a series of annual maximum flows, and regional data let ungauged reaches be estimated indirectly.

Floods are not only a loss. Smaller, more frequent floods can recharge groundwater and make soil more fertile, and periodic flooding was essential to ancient peoples along the Nile, Indus and other rivers.

nature-nbs-326.title: Drinking water: safe to swallow
nature-nbs-326.text:
Contaminated water is estimated to cause more than half a million deaths a year; in 2011 infectious diarrhea killed about 0.7 million children under five. Drinking water is water that is safe to ingest, whether drunk directly or used in food preparation. Safe water, per the WHO 2017 report, poses no significant health risk over a lifetime of consumption. Its quality parameters fall into microbiological, chemical and physical groups, and fecal coliforms such as E. coli indicate sewage contamination.

No universally accepted international standards exist, and permitted concentrations can differ up to ten times between standards. Sixty million people are estimated to have been poisoned by fluoride-contaminated well water.

Progress has been real. Access to improved sources rose from 76 percent in 1990 to 91 percent by 2015, tracked by the WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Program. In the United States only 1% of public supply goes to drinking and cooking; typical home use is 69.3 US gallons per person per day.

nature-nbs-319.title: Dams: holding back rivers
nature-nbs-319.text:
There were 62,362 large dams worldwide in 2025, and an estimated 2.8 million human-made dams of any size in 2019. A dam is a structure that impounds water or restricts its flow. Dams provide irrigation, hydropower, water supply, flood management, recreation, inland navigation and fish farming, and many multi-purpose dams serve two or more of these. Human-made dams are classed as embankment, gravity, buttress, arch or composite; natural dams include rockslide, volcanic and beaver dams.

The costs are real. Dams can alter rivers, habitats, vegetation, biodiversity and microclimates, and often degrade downstream water quality and volume, especially in the dry season. Developers in many countries must prepare an {{ref:nature-pol-132}} so the government can judge a dam's desirability, mitigate impacts and compensate affected people. Reservoirs gradually accumulate sediment, which cuts storage capacity and so the dam's ability to irrigate, generate power or control floods. A dam may be removed if it is a safety hazard, no longer serves its purpose, or to restore fish migration and downstream river health.

nature-nbs-330.title: Levees: ridges that keep rivers in their beds
nature-nbs-330.text:
The Mississippi levee system has over 5,600 km of levees, averaging 7.3 m high by the mid-1980s, with some as high as 15 m. A levee is an elevated ridge alongside a river, often built to protect the adjoining area from flooding. Also called a dike, dyke, floodbank or stop bank, it is usually earthen and runs along a river in its floodplain or along low-lying coasts.

Artificial levees prevent flooding of adjoining land and slow channel changes to keep shipping lanes reliable. But they confine the river, so flow is higher and faster. A levee is only as strong as its weakest point, so its height and construction standard must be consistent along its length.

Designs vary. In the Bay of Fundy marshlands, Acadian dykes use hinged sluice gates (aboiteaux) that drain fresh water on the falling tide and close on the rising tide. Levees in the Netherlands have gone beyond defence, taking back land below mean sea level.

nature-nbs-325.title: Detention basins: storing a storm and releasing it slowly
nature-nbs-325.text:
A detention basin is an excavated area on or near a waterway that protects against flooding, and sometimes downstream erosion, by temporarily storing water. It lets large flows in and limits outflow through a small low opening sized to downstream culvert capacity, and it can control events such as a 1-in-100-year storm. Basins are usually built with new developments to handle runoff from impervious surfaces like roads, parking lots and rooftops.

A basin with no permanent pool is a dry pond. One designed to hold some water permanently is a retention basin, which manages quantity but has limited effect on water quality. Real-time control of outflow makes basins significantly better at retaining suspended solids and associated contaminants. Extended detention dry basins lengthen storage time beyond the 6 to 12 hours of basic ponds, allowing more settling of solids and cleaner water.

Urban parks can serve as dual-purpose basins, acting as sports fields or parkland normally and storing stormwater in big storms; Joynton Park in Sydney is an example.

nature-nbs-322.title: Combined sewers: one pipe for sewage and rain
nature-nbs-322.text:
About 860 US communities have combined sewers, serving about 40 million people; the UK has about 22,000 overflows. A combined sewer is a gravity sewer system that carries sewage and urban stormwater runoff together to a treatment plant or disposal site. In rain, sewage is diluted and flows at the treatment site rise. Runoff can pick up sediment, heavy metals, organic compounds, animal waste, and oil and grease.

Combined sewer overflows occur when combined flow exceeds what the treatment plant or sewer can carry. The design has old roots. Early sewers carried street runoff untreated into waterways, and before 19th-century macadam paving, porous surfaces let rain soak away. The link to {{ref:nature-res-261}} is direct, and {{ref:nature-nbs-161}} is one way to reduce the load.

nature-nbs-323.title: Combined sewer overflows: when the pipe cannot cope
nature-nbs-323.text:
In 2024 the UK Environment Agency recorded 445,297 spills from overflows totalling 3,582,658 hours. A combined sewer overflow is a relief structure, and the discharge event it causes, diverting flow beyond a combined sewer's treatment capacity into waterways. Europe is estimated to have more than 628,000 overflows.

Discharges carry human and industrial waste and can close beaches, restrict shellfish consumption and contaminate drinking water sources. In the United States the pollutants include pathogens, toxic chemicals and debris, linked to antimicrobial resistance, and the EPA required improvements in a 1994 policy.

Sanitary sewer overflows differ. They come from blockages, damage or excess flow, can occur at any low spot, and may be worse in dry weather with no runoff to dilute them.
